title: 3. Lambda architecture
summary: A batch layer for correctness, a speed layer for freshness and a serving layer that merges them: how it works, why dual code paths hurt, and why most teams moved on.

blocks.text: 39.1 Context and the problem it solved

In the early 2010s, batch systems (Hadoop MapReduce, Hive) could process petabytes correctly but took hours. Stream processors of that time (Storm, early Spark Streaming) were fast but had weak guarantees: at-least-once delivery, no robust state management, and trouble with late or out-of-order events (chapter 6). Nobody trusted a streaming job to produce the number finance would sign off.

Lambda, described by Nathan Marz around 2011, answers by running both. The **batch layer** recomputes views from the complete, immutable master dataset, so any bug or approximation is eventually corrected. The **speed layer** processes only recent data to cover the hours since the last batch run. The **serving layer** merges both at query time. The guiding principle is that data is immutable and every view is a function of all data: `view = function(all data)`.
The name refers to lambda calculus and pure functions over immutable data, not to AWS Lambda. Mixing the two up in an interview is a common slip.
39.2 Reference diagram

Every event is written to two places. The **batch layer** appends it to the master dataset (HDFS or object storage) and, on a schedule, recomputes the batch views from scratch or over large windows. The **speed layer** updates realtime views incrementally as events arrive. When a batch run completes up to time T, the speed layer's state for data before T is discarded, because the batch view now covers it.

A query for 'page views today' reads the batch view up to T (say, midnight or the last completed run) and adds the realtime view from T to now. The speed layer therefore only ever has to be *approximately* right for a few hours; errors are self-healing at the next batch run.

blocks.text: **Where Iceberg, Snowflake and semantic models fit.** Today the batch layer would naturally be Iceberg tables, whose snapshots make the master dataset and its recomputations reproducible. Snowflake can host the batch views, and with Snowpipe Streaming or dynamic tables it can absorb part of the speed layer, which removes the need for a separate merge service (check current documentation for latency guarantees). A semantic model fits only on the merged result; defining metrics separately on each path guarantees divergence.

blocks.text: The merge only works if both views have **identical keys and compatible measures**. Additive measures (counts, sums) merge by addition across disjoint time ranges. Distinct counts do not add: unique users in batch plus unique users in speed double-counts anyone active in both. Teams used mergeable sketches such as HyperLogLog for those.

blocks.title: Serving-layer merge expressed in SQL (Postgres dialect)
blocks.text:
-- batch_pageviews covers hours < :cutover; rt_pageviews covers hours >= :cutover
SELECT page_id, SUM(views) AS views
FROM (
  SELECT page_id, views FROM batch_pageviews
  WHERE  event_hour <  :cutover AND event_hour >= date_trunc('day', now())
  UNION ALL
  SELECT page_id, views FROM rt_pageviews
  WHERE  event_hour >= :cutover
) v
GROUP BY page_id;

The cutover timestamp must be exactly the boundary that the last successful batch run covered. If it is taken from the clock instead of the batch run's metadata, a delayed batch leaves a gap or an overlap, and numbers jump when the next run lands.
39.5 Ingestion, orchestration and serving

steps.label: Swap views
steps.sub: advance cutover, drop old realtime state

blocks.text: Orchestration spans two worlds. The batch side is a scheduled DAG (Oozie, then Airflow) that recomputes views and, on success, publishes a new cutover marker. The speed side is a long-running streaming job managed like a service, with its own deployment, monitoring and restart logic. The swap step must be coordinated: publish the new batch view, move the cutover, then expire realtime state older than it.

blocks.text: Teams moved away for three reasons. First, stream processors matured: Flink and Kafka Streams offered exactly-once state, event-time windows and watermarks (chapter 20), so the speed layer could be trusted. Second, unified engines (Spark Structured Streaming, Flink, Beam) let one code base run in batch and streaming mode. Third, table formats and warehouses gained efficient incremental upserts, so micro-batches every few minutes (chapter 19) often met the freshness need with a single path.
39.7 When to choose it / when not

items: **Consider it** when the fast path must use an approximate or cheap algorithm (sketches, sampling) and an exact batch recomputation must eventually replace it, for example billing or ad attribution with preliminary real-time figures.
**Consider it** when the batch computation is fundamentally different from what can run incrementally, such as ML model retraining over full history alongside online feature updates.
**Avoid it** when one engine can run the same logic in streaming and batch mode; use Kappa (chapter 40) or a unified engine.
**Avoid it** when 5 to 15 minute freshness is enough; micro-batch into one table instead.
**Avoid it** with a small team: two paths double the on-call surface.
**If you keep it**, share the business logic as a library or SQL definitions used by both paths, and test that both produce equal results on the same input.

blocks.title: Ad-tech impressions and billing
blocks.text: An ad platform shows advertisers live spend dashboards and invoices them monthly. The speed layer (Flink) counts impressions and spend per campaign per minute with at-least-once semantics and HyperLogLog for unique reach. The batch layer (Spark over Iceberg) runs hourly and nightly, deduplicates by impression id, removes bot traffic using a model that needs a full day of data, and produces the billable numbers.
items: Live dashboards read speed results for the current hour, merged with hourly batch for earlier hours.
Invoices use only the nightly batch view; the dashboard labels recent hours 'preliminary'.
A reconciliation job compares speed and batch totals per hour and alerts if the gap exceeds 2 percent.

blocks.title: Retire one speed layer
blocks.text: A team runs Lambda for an e-commerce 'orders per minute' dashboard: Storm for speed, nightly Hive for batch, Cassandra for serving. Freshness required by the business is 5 minutes. Propose a migration to a single path. Decide what replaces each layer, how you prove the new path matches the old batch numbers, how you handle the cutover period, and which parts of Lambda (if any) you keep.
hints: Is 5 minutes a streaming requirement or a micro-batch one?
Run old and new in parallel and compare per-hour totals.
Late and corrected orders must still be handled somewhere.

items: Lambda runs a batch layer for correctness and a speed layer for freshness, merged in a serving layer.
The master dataset is immutable; batch views are recomputed and replace realtime views at each cutover.
The merge needs identical keys, a precise cutover marker and care with non-additive measures.
The core cost is two implementations of the same logic, with drift and double operations.
It still fits when the fast path is deliberately approximate and an exact batch result must win.

blocks.q: In Lambda architecture, what happens to speed-layer results once a batch run covering that period completes?
options: They are merged permanently into the master dataset
They are discarded, because the batch view now covers that period
They are used to validate the batch run and then archived as the source of truth
They are kept and summed with the batch view to improve accuracy
blocks.explain: The speed layer only covers the gap since the last batch run. Keeping and summing it with the batch view would double count; the master dataset holds raw events, not derived views.

blocks.q: Why can't you simply add 'unique users' from the batch view and the realtime view?
options: The serving layer only supports SUM on integer columns
Realtime views cannot compute distinct counts at all
Distinct counts are not additive; users active in both periods would be counted twice
The batch view stores users in a different data type
blocks.explain: Counts and sums over disjoint ranges add up; distinct counts do not. Mergeable sketches such as HyperLogLog are the usual fix. Speed layers can compute distinct counts, so "realtime views cannot compute distinct counts" is wrong.

blocks.q: Which development most reduced the need for Lambda architecture?
options: Stream processors with exactly-once state and event-time handling, plus engines that run one code base in batch and streaming mode
The move from MapReduce to Hive
The invention of the star schema
blocks.explain: Lambda existed because streaming results could not be trusted and batch was slow. Trustworthy streaming and unified engines remove the need for a second path; cheaper storage or Hive did not change that.

blocks.q: A Lambda system shows a sudden jump in today's totals every morning at 03:00. What is the most likely cause?
options: The speed layer is running exactly-once
The batch layer is using Parquet instead of Avro
Batch and speed logic differ (or the cutover is misaligned), so replacing realtime results with batch results changes the number
blocks.explain: A jump at swap time means the two paths disagree, either through logic drift or a cutover gap or overlap. File format and Kafka retention do not cause a step change at the batch completion time.
